title: Axe-Head-Shaped Piezoelectric Energy Harvesters Designed for Base and Tip Excitation-Based Energy Scavenging
venue: IEEE Transactions on Ultrasonics, Ferroelectrics and Frequency Control

sections.heading: Axe-Head Shaped Piezoelectric Energy Harvesters Designed for Base and Tip Excitation Based Energy Scavenging
sections.text:
Bapi Debnath, Student Member, IEEE, and R. Kumar

Abstract—In this article, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) ferroelectric polymer thin film-based two Axe-Head shaped cantilever type piezoelectric energy harvester (C-PEH) devices are presented, such as Device-1.1 with ring proof mass and another Device-2.1 without ring proof mass for base excitation and tip excitation based energy harvesting, respectively. These fabricated miniature Axe-Head shaped C-PEHs comprising different active area and volume are evaluated by both finite element method (FEM) based simulations and experimentations. We also present a concept to use these prototypes in a wireless mouse to harvest base and tip excitation based energy. Device-1.1 made with $\mathbf { 9 6 . 5 \ m m ^ { 3 } }$ active volume including an Axe-Head shaped C-PEH and a 0.72 gram ring proof mass produces maximum ${ \bf 7 . 8 1 n W }$ and ${ \bf 5 9 4 . 5 \ n W }$ power outputs when it was excited by $\mathbf { X }$ -axis (direction of normal wireless mouse sliding) and $\mathbf { Z }$ -axis (direction of gravity entailing $\mathbf { 0 . 5 8 }$ acceleration) based vibrations, respectively. Device-2.1 made with $\mathbf { 1 4 . 8 \ m m ^ { 3 } }$ active volume comprising only an Axe-Head shaped C-PEH produces maximum $9 . 3 3 9 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ and $\mathbf { 0 . 0 3 6 9 \mu W }$ power outputs when it was excited by a rotary motion due to a wireless mouse-wheel rotation and $\mathbf { Z }$ -axis (direction of gravity entailing 0.5 g acceleration) based vibration, respectively. The experimental results demonstrate excellent performance when compared to the test results of the well-known same active area and volume based trapezoidal shaped C-PEHs, and other already published similar devices.

Index Terms— Energy harvester, piezoelectric, PVDF, Axe-Head shaped, resonant frequency, FEM, COMSOL, PEH.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
OWADYS, with the recent advancements of ultra-low power consumable electronics, the piezoelectric based N energy scavenging has gain a huge research consideration. The main advantage of using piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) into a system is that a battery itself or else externally charging a battery may become unnecessary. Various types of PEHs have been explored because it has prominent energy conversion efficiency, simple configuration property, and does not required any extra power supply.

Tao et al. [1] introduced a microelectromechanical system (MEMS) based PEH having two-degree-of-freedom characteristics and ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ piezoelectric material. This proposed

PEH system consists two subsystems, the first one used for energy scavenging and the second one used for frequency adjustment. Wang et al. [2] demonstrated a method for mechanical-vibration based power scavenging using serially and parallelly connected array of four PZT piezoelectric material based circular membranes. These proposed PEHs were able to generate $2 8 ~ \mathrm { \ m W }$ and $2 7 ~ \mathrm { \ m W }$ power while four membranes were connected in series and parallel, respectively. Koven et al. [3] presented a base mounted PEH in which PZT-5H piezoelectric material placed underneath of the cantileverbased resonator beam. This experimentally validated PEH generates a $4 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ resonance based average power of $8 . 7 5 \ \mu \mathrm { W }$ and $1 1 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at $0 . 2 5 \mathrm { g }$ and $1 . 0 \mathrm { g }$ accelerations, respectively. Wang et al. [4] proposed a cross-tunnel structure based PEH comprising fluoroethylenepropylene piezoelectret flexible films. This investigated PEH was able to produce $3 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 2 }$ power at $6 5 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ vibrational frequency. Pondrom et al. [5] investigated PEHs with single-layer and stacked (multiplelayer) piezoelectret films. In this proposed method power was generated by the accelerating proof mass induced stress. Berdy et al. [6] achieved $1 1 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ power output at $4 9 . 7 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ (frequency) and $0 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ (acceleration) using a PZT piezoelectric material based bimorph meandering PEH. Song et al. [7] demonstrated a spiral shaped MEMS based unimorph vibration-PEH which generates $2 3 . 3 \mathrm { ~ \ n W }$ at $6 8 \mathrm { H z }$ (frequency) and $0 . 2 5 \textrm { \text g }$ (acceleration). Park et al. [8] explored the ${ \bf d } _ { 3 3 }$ -mode (also known as interdigitated-style) of the PZT piezoelectric material based PEH. This investigated PEH generates $1 . 1 \mu \mathrm { W }$ power at $5 2 8 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ (frequency) and $0 . 3 9 \mathrm { g }$ (acceleration). Liu et al. [9] microfabricated a S-shaped base vibration based PEH comprising the ${ \bf d } _ { 3 1 }$ -mode (also known as capacitor-style) of PZT piezoelectric material. The tested prototype was able to generate $1 . 1 1 7 \mathrm { n W }$ power at $2 7 . 4 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ frequency. Park et al. [10] proposed a new design of cantilever based PEH, in which power is produced by the rotary motion-based excitation applied on the free tip end of the PEH. Kuang et al. [11] demonstrated a mechanically plucked PEH utilizing plastic plectra for plucking the PZT piezoelectric material based cantilevers. Literature survey indicates that cantilever type PEH (C-PEH) has been investigated and studied intensively because of its simplicity and microfabrication feasibility [12], [13]. According to many researchers, the most optimized shaped C-PEH is tapered or trapezoidal shaped C-PEH [14]–[22].

In this paper, we are proposing two devices (i.e. Device-1.1 Device-2.1) comprising novel Axe-Head shaped C-PEH designs in which Device-1.1 consist an Axe-Head shaped C-PEH with ring proof mass at the free end of C-PEH for base excitation based energy scavenging and Device-2.1 only consist an Axe-Head shaped C-PEH without any proof mass for tip excitation based energy scavenging. Most of the reported C-PEHs had used lead zirconate titanate (PZT) piezoelectric material for their energy scavenging purpose but we have used polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) in our proposed C-PEHs. Because PVDF is environmentally friendly lead-free ferroelectric polymer. Also compared to piezoceramics like PZT, piezoelectric polymers like PVDF are nonfragile and can bear large deformation [23].

The proposed C-PEHs are analyzed by both finite element method (FEM) software COMSOL Multiphysics based simulations and experimental measurements. We compared the outcomes of the proposed C-PEHs with highly identical active area and volume based most popular trapezoidal shaped C-PEHs, for instance, Device-1.1 compared with Device-1.2 comprising ring proof mass in trapezoidal shaped C-PEH and Device-2.1 compared with Device-2.2 comprising only trapezoidal shaped C-PEH without ring proof mass. We also compared the power outputs with previously reported PEHs [24]–[26].

sections.heading: II. DESIGN CONCEPT & WORKING PRINCIPLE
sections.text:
It is well-known that whenever piezoelectric material is mechanically strained it produces electrical voltage and vice versa. This fact is very useful to generate electrical energy from a C-PEH device by making it vibrated or displaced. The power output produced by the deformation of piezoelectric structure is subjected to the effective electrode area of piezoelectric materials. For a unimorph cantilever comprising piezoelectric material, the produced output power can be determined from the expression [7]: $$ \tilde { P _ { o u t p u t } } = f \cdot S ^ { 2 } \cdot V _ { p } \cdot E _ { p } \cdot k _ { x y } ^ { 2 } $$ and $$ k _ { x y } ^ { 2 } = \frac { S t o r e d e n e r g y } { I n p u t m e c h a n i c a l e n e r g y } = \frac { E _ { p } d _ { x y } ^ { 2 } } { \varepsilon } $$ where $f$ is excitation frequency $( \mathrm { H z } ) , S$ is strain, $V _ { p }$ is volume of the piezoelectric material, $E _ { p }$ is Young’s modulus, $\varepsilon$ is dielectric permittivity, $d _ { x y }$ is piezoelectric constant and $k _ { x y }$ is electromechanical coupling coefficient by means of $\mathbf { X }$ -poling and y-applied stress direction. Equation (1) is confirming that C-PEH generated power is proportional to the involved strain and it can be fed to the device by employing cantilever tip excitation or else base excitation. According to the previous reports, the C-PEH can produce maximal power at its resonant frequency [6]. The natural frequency $\left( \omega _ { \mathrm { n } } \right)$ of any cantilever beam in transverse vibration can be expressed as [6]: $$ \omega _ { n } = \sqrt { \frac { k _ { e q } } { m _ { e q } } } = \sqrt { \frac { 3 E I / L ^ { 3 } } { ( 3 3 / 1 4 0 ) M _ { b } L + M _ { m } } } $$ where $m _ { e q }$ and $k _ { e q }$ are effective mass and spring constant of the structure, respectively. $E I$ and $L$ are flexural rigidity and length of the beam, respectively. $M _ { b }$ represents the mass per unit length, and $M _ { m }$ represents the tip mass. Exploiting Equations (1) and (2), we can corroborate that the formation of the electrical potential in the C-PEH device is directly associated to the stress stimulated by the relative deformation. Therefore, in order to exploit the overall stress stimulated by the relative deformation, we proposed Axe-Head shaped composite cantilever designs. The proposed Axe-Head shaped cantilevers are designed in that way so that they can utilize maximum stimulated stress over tip ends (i.e. both the free end and the clamped end of the cantilever) to generate efficient electricity. In order to harvest the base and tip excitation based energy, we proposed two novel Axe-Head shaped C-PEH device designs such as Device-1.1 for base excitation and Device-2.1 for tip excitation based energy scavenging. To compare the outcomes with the well-known trapezoidal shaped C-PEH devices, we also prepared highly equivalent active area and volume based two trapezoidal shaped C-PEH devices such that Device-1.2 entailing highly equivalent active area $( 3 7 . 1 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 } )$ and volume $( 9 6 . 5 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 } )$ ) as Device-1.1, and Device-2.2 entailing highly equivalent active area $( 8 0 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 } )$ ) and volume $( 1 4 . 8 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 } )$ as Device-2.1. To reduce the natural frequency of the Device-1.1, 1.2 C-PEHs, a brass ring proof mass entailing $6 \ \mathrm { m m }$ thickness and $1 4 . 9 4 8 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ area is used at the free end of the cantilevers. A 3-dimensional (3D) schematic model and indetail device geometrical dimensions of the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2 are shown in Fig. 1. The values of the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1, and 2.2 geometrical parameters are given in Table 1. In order to design the PEH based electrodes for charge collection, two piezoelectric modes, such as ${ \bf d } _ { 3 1 }$ [27] and ${ \mathrm { d } } _ { 3 3 }$ [28], can be employed. We utilized the ${ \bf d } _ { 3 1 }$ mode since it entails simple electrode-construction compare to the ${ \mathrm { d } } _ { 3 3 }$ mode for cantilever type PEH. Fig. 1 (a)–(d) shows the cross-section view of the composite cantilever used in the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1, and 2.2. As depicted in Fig. 1 (a)–(d), the cantilevers consist a sandwich structure of PVDF $2 8 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ piezoelectric material between two silver electrodes $( 9 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ , which is patterned on the top a mylar polyester substrate layer $1 2 5 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ and covered by a protective acrylic layer $( 1 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ . When base excitation based vibration is employed to the Device-1.1 and tip excitation based force is applied to the tip of the Device-2.1, free ends of the C-PEHs will move moderately. Consequently, the resulting stress on the PVDF piezoelectric layers will generate electrical potential. ![](images/609dbf49aee21a23d8ba6af6b9ccb2b0ac52bc470d2caede9be51adafbdfd4f7.jpg) ![](images/dfaa88dfff0b01ee53f28c439d702b22ab13e6c6858203ba7541c4c2abdb685d.jpg) Fig. 1. To demonstrate one application of the proposed C-PEHs, a concept based schematic model to recharge the battery in a wireless mouse is illustrated in Fig. 2. The base and tip excitation sources generating from a normal wireless mouse inuse situation was considered such as: (i) generating the base excitation-based source when we normally move a mouse, and (ii) generating the tip excitation-based source when we mechanically rotate a mouse wheel. Liu et al. [29] demonstrated that an array of PEH can improve the power output. Hence, for a self-sustained wireless mouse, an array of Axe-Head shaped PEHs consisting mass can be used for different axis based base excitation harvesting and an array of PEHs without mass can be used for tip excitation energy harvesting. However, in this paper, for the sake of simplicity in fabrication and validation process of the proposed novel C-PEH designs, we investigated only single-single base and tip excitation based C-PEHs instead of an array of C-PEHs. sections.heading: A. Finite Element Method (FEM) Simulation
sections.text: To determine the optimum size and shape of the PEH devices before fabrication, optimization was done by FEM simulations through the commercial package of COMSOL Multiphysics 5.4 software. FEM based model of PEH Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 are designed and simulated in COMSOL 3D plane. These devices consist PVDF piezoelectric material based unimorph cantilever structure which is fixed from one end and free from another end. The mechanical and electrical responses of the COMSOL modeled devices are established by collaborating Solid Mechanics (solid), Electrostatics (es) and Electrical Circuits (cir) physics in Multiphysics of Piezoelectric Devices (pze1). Due to gravity the C-PEH structures are confronted with the pre-bending condition which can be employ in terms of Body Load in Solid Mechanics (solid). Also, in the Solid Mechanics (solid) physics, a condition of sinusoidal acceleration can be employed to generate strain in the PVDF ferroelectric polymer layer. In Electrostatics (es) physics, the voltage accumulation is carried out by employing the Ground and Terminal Boundary condition on the PVDF layer. Material properties, for instance Young’s modulus, dielectric permittivities, and piezoelectric coefficients etc. used for the simulations are based on the data presented in the LDT0-028K and LDTM-028K/L data sheets [30], [31]. The Mesh element size in COMSOL modeled devices are reduced up to saturated simulating results. Initially different element sizes of meshing were tried, finally optimal Free Triangular and Tetrahedral blocks with finest element size are used for the PEH models. COMSOL based parametric studies, for instance, Stationery study, Eigenfrequency study and Frequency Domain study are performed to observe and evaluate the stress distribution over deformation, resonant frequencies and electrical responses of the modeled devices, respectively.

sections.heading: B. Prototype fabrication
sections.text:
Fig. 3 depicts the schematics of the fabricated Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2 prototypes which were prepared with geometric properties listed in Table-1 and Fig. 1. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed C-PEHs, prototypes were fabricated by utilizing the commercially available LDT0-028K and LDTM-028K (Sensor Solutions-TE Connectivity) piezoelectric sensor beams which comprises a PVDF piezoelectric thin film of ${ \sim } 2 8 \ \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ with screen-printed $\mathbf { A } \mathbf { g }$ (silver)-ink electrodes and a mylar polyester substrate of ${ \sim } 1 2 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . Each used beam consists two crimped contacts which were attached to top and bottom Ag-electrodes, to accrue the power output due to beam displacements. Precise cutting machine tools were employed on LDT0-028K and LDTM-028K beams to prepare the Axe-Head shaped and tapered shaped C-PEHs. To develop the Device-1.1 and 1.2 the LDT0- 028K beams were used. And the Device-2.1 and 2.2 were prepared by utilizing the LDTM-028K beams embedded with brass proof mass of 0.72 gram at the free end. The crosssectional microscopic image of the used beams is shown in Fig. 3 (e).

sections.heading: IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND PROCEDURE
sections.text:
The experimental measurements and verifications of the presented C-PEH designs are performed utilizing five experimental platforms (EPs). Fig. 4–8 shows the schematic drawing and photographs of EP-1–5, respectively. In order to collect the real time vibration data due to motion of the wireless mouse towards $\mathbf { X }$ or Y-direction, the EP-1 is used which includes a 3-axis acceleration sensor (ADXL327) mounted on a wireless mouse. To measure the real time tip excitation based data due to the wireless mouse wheel rotation, the EP-2 is used which comprises a stage to hold a vibration sensor (LDT0- 028K) and a rotating gear having the physical properties listed in Table-2. In order to measure real time outputs of the presented C-PEHs for base excitation based vibration due to sliding of the assembled mechanism towards X-direction, the EP-3 is used. As depicted in Fig. 6 inset, the assembled mechanism used in this EP-3 can hold the C-PEHs either towards upwards direction or downwards direction. The EP-4 is used to verify the outcomes from the presented C-PEHs for tip excitation based harvesting. For outcome verifications of the presented C-PEHs at their respective resonant frequency, the EP-5 is used which includes a vibrator incorporated with a C-PEH holding stage, a inbuilt waveform generator in Digilent Analog Discovery 2 for supplying the required magnitude and frequency input to the vibrator, an accelerometer (ADXL327) for measuring the vibrator generated acceleration, and an inbuilt oscilloscope in Digilent Analog Discovery 2 for measuring the electrical output from the C-PEHs..In EP-5, the $\mathrm { _ { Z } }$ -direction based vibration is employed the devices whereas Z-direction represents the gravity direction. The generated electrical outputs flowing from the presented C-PEHs to the electric circuit comprising external load resistor are collected across that resistor using Digilent Analog Discovery 2 linked to a PC comprising WaveForms software. In order to collect the acceleration value from ADXL327, a data acquisition (DAQ) system is utilized. Used DAQ system comprises a NI 9232 DAQ card and a NI cDAQ-9178 chassis allied to a LabView-National Instruments software installed Desktop Computer.

sections.heading: A. Simulation and experimental evaluation
sections.text:
Employing EP-1, the real time vibration data due to normal speed of motion of the wireless mouse towards X and $\mathrm { Y }$ -axes has been collected using an accelerometer at the rate of 12.8 kHz sampling frequency and $2 5 6 0 0 / \mathrm { s e c }$ data sample. Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) technique is used to evaluate the frequency spectrum of the collected vibration data. Due to X and Y-axes direction based movement of the mouse, Fig. 9 (a), (b) shows the time domain signature of the acquired vibration data and Fig. 9 (c), (d) shows frequency spectrum of the acquired vibration data (zoomed view near high peak-frequency range), respectively. Fig. 9 (a) and (b) demonstrates that both X and Y- axes has almost same peak acceleration i.e. $0 . 6 3 \mathrm { g }$ , $0 . 5 3 \mathrm { g }$ , respectively. Fig. 9 (c) and (d) demonstrates that both X and Yaxes has almost same peak frequency range i.e. below $4 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . Hence, we choose only $\mathbf { X }$ -axis based direction to evaluate the performance of our proposed C-PEH device but in real time application two or more number of C-PEH can be used for different axis based energy harvesting. We also investigate the peak acceleration and frequency generated due to X-axis based wireless mouse movement 20 times and the measured results show that average peak acceleration and frequency lies between the range of $0 . 4 \mathrm { - } 0 . 6 \mathrm { g }$ and $1 0 { - } 3 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , respectively. Therefore, for this kind of low acceleration and frequency range based environment, we proposed Axe-Head shaped Device1.1 C-PEH which can produce improved power output compare to Device-1.2 comprising most popular trapezoidal shaped C-PEH.

![](images/3a75fd8c99155e00b3e6d53e51cb846646a7288646b9123b88551eb7c53b4419.jpg)  
Fig. 9. Acceleration signature of the mouse movement towards (a) X-axis based direction, (b) Y-axis based direction, and zoomed view near the high peakfrequency range of the FFT of the acceleration signature obtained from the mouse movement towards (c) X-axis based direction, (d) Y-axis based direction.

Employing EP-5, the real time tip excitation based data due to rotation of the gear (comprising the dimensions as tabulated in Table 2) of the wireless mouse in clockwise and anticlockwise has been collected using an a vibration sensor (LDT0-028K) having $8 0 0 \ \mathrm { m V / g }$ sensitivity. FFT is used to evaluate the frequency spectrum of the collected data. Due to clockwise and anticlockwise rotation of the mouse wheel-gear, Fig. 10 (a), (b) shows the time domain signature of the acquired data and Fig. 10 (c), (d) shows frequency spectrum of the acquired vibration data (zoomed view near peak-frequency range). Fig. 10 (a) and (b) demonstrates that both clockwise and anticlockwise has almost same peak acceleration i.e. $1 1 . 1 \ \mathrm { g }$ $1 1 . 4 \ \mathrm { g }$ , respectively. And Fig. 10 (c) and (d) demonstrates that both X and $\mathrm { Y } \mathrm { - }$ axes has almost same peak frequency range i.e. first range $1 { - } 4 5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ and second range $5 0 0 { - } 2 0 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Hence, we choose only clockwise based direction to evaluate the performance of our proposed C-PEH device. We also investigate the peak acceleration and frequency generated due to clockwise based wireless mouse gear rotation 20 times and the measured results show that average peak acceleration and frequency lies between the range of $8 \mathrm { - } 1 2 \mathrm { g }$ and $1 { - } 5 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ respectively. Therefore, for this kind of tip excitation based acceleration and frequency range, we proposed Axe-Head shaped Device-2.1 which can produce improved power output compare to Device-2.2 comprising most popular trapezoidal shaped C-PEH. Due to clockwise rotation, the resultant tip displacement is measured to be ${ \sim } 6 \mathrm { m m }$ .

peak-frequency range of the FFT of the acceleration signature obtained from the mouse wheel rotation towards (c) clockwise direction, (d) anticlockwise direction.

In order to investigate the natural frequency of the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2, we used FEM simulator COMSOL Multiphysics 5.4 (commercial version). Simulated mode shapes over 1st natural frequency of the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 are shown in Fig. 11 (a)–(d), respectively. These results show an up-down tip-displacement of the C-PEHs entailing 24.114 Hz, 24.447 Hz, $3 7 0 . 9 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , and $4 4 2 . 2 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ natural frequency for the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2, respectively.

In order to investigate the stress concentration of the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2, we employed 1MPa boundary load on top surface of the devices using FEM simulator COMSOL Multiphysics 5.4 (commercial version). Resulting model of the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 are shown in Fig. 12 (a)–(d), respectively. These results show that incase of both the Device-1.1 and 2.1, the maximum area of the Axe-Head shaped composite cantilevers experiences high but fairly distributed stress compare to the Device-1.2 and 2.2 entailing most popular trapezoidal shaped composite cantilever, which will contribute to generate more electrical output.

EP-6 is used to collect the base excitation based real time electrical response until 5 seconds each for the Device-1.1 and 1.2 (with a $1 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ fixed load resistance) due to sliding of the assembled stage-mechanism towards X-direction. For instance, Fig. 13 (a) shows the X-axis movement of the mouse and Fig. 13 (b) demonstrates the resultant outcome of the Device-1.1 C-

PEH while keeping the free end proof mass towards upwards direction. As demonstrated in Fig. 14, we also investigated the outcome of the Device-1.1 C-PEH while keeping the free end proof mass towards downwards direction but end proof mass towards upwards direction shows maximum voltage and power output of $8 8 . 4 1 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ and $7 . 8 1 \ \mathrm { n W }$ compare to $7 5 . 4 7 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ and $5 . 6 9 \ \mathrm { n W }$ entailing downwards direction, respectively. Fig. 14 (a) shows the $\mathbf { X }$ -axis movement of the mouse while keeping the free end proof mass towards downwards direction and Fig. 14 (b) demonstrates the resultant outcome of the Device-1.1 C-PEH. Furthermore, for the Device-1.2 C-PEH, we investigated the outcome of the device while keeping the free end proof mass towards upwards direction. Corresponding mouse movement is shown in in Fig. 15 (a) and resultant outcome illustrated in Fig. 15 (b), which shows maximum voltage and power output of $7 2 . 8 7 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ and $5 . 3 1 \mathrm { \ n W }$ , respectively. From Fig. 13–15, it is observed that the Device-1.1 comprising an Axe-Head shaped C-PEH with ring mass demonstrates more electrical output for base-based excitation, than the Device-1.2 comprising a wellknown trapezoidal shaped C-PEH with ring mass.

EP-7 is used to collect the tip excitation based real time electrical response until 5 seconds each for the Device-2.1 and 2.2 due to the clockwise rotation of wireless mouse gear at constant 1 MΩ load resistance. For instance, Fig. 16 (a) shows the photo of clockwise rotation of the gear and Fig. 16 (b) demonstrates the resultant outcome of the Device-2.1 C-PEH. And Fig. 17 (a) shows the photo of clockwise rotation of the gear and Fig. 17 (b) demonstrates the resultant outcome of the Device-2.2 C-PEH. Employing FEM simulator COMSOL and EP-8, we also investigated the maximum power generation capability of the devices when the excitation frequency matches with the device natural frequency while normally moving the mouse. And the measured peak voltage output is 771.02 mV, $7 5 3 . 0 3 \mathrm { ~ m V }$ , $1 9 1 . 9 8 \mathrm { ~ m V }$ , $1 9 2 . 9 8 \mathrm { ~ m V }$ and peak power output is $5 9 4 . 4 7 { \mathrm { ~ n W } }$ , $5 6 7 . 0 6 \mathrm { n W }$ , $3 7 . 2 4 { \mathrm { ~ n W } }$ , $3 3 . 6 7 \ \mathrm { n W }$ for the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2 at resonant frequency of 24.1 Hz, 24.4 Hz, $3 7 0 . 9 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $4 4 2 . 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , respectively. The measured peak power is $5 9 4 . 5 \ \mathrm { n W }$ , $5 6 7 . 1 \ \mathrm { n W }$ , 36.9 nW, $3 3 . 7 \mathrm { n W }$ and voltage output is $8 4 4 . 6 \mathrm { m V }$ , $8 2 4 . 9 \mathrm { m V }$ , 210.5 mV, $2 0 1 . 2 \mathrm { m V }$ for the Device-1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2 at optimal load resistance of $1 . 2 ~ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ (for all devices), respectively. sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.text:
In this paper, two different active area and volume based C-PEH devices such that Device-1.1 and 2.1 but comprising the same Axe-Head shaped composite cantilever based structure concept for the base and tip excitation based energy harvesting, respectively are designed, simulated and fabricated. An envirofriendly PVDF piezoelectric material was employed to generate charge from vibration via piezoelectric effect and it was sandwiched between two silver electrodes for the generated charge accumulation purpose. Using suitable experimental setups, the potential generation capability of the fabricated C-PEHs was investigated. The Device 1.1 and 2.1 generates peak $7 . 8 1 \ \mathrm { n W }$ , $9 . 3 3 9 1 \mu \mathrm { W }$ electric power and peak $8 8 . 4 1 \mathrm { m V }$ , 3.056 V electrical voltage when subjected to base and tip excitation based mechanical vibrations due to the normal movement of a wireless mouse and mouse-wheel rotation, respectively. When the input acceleration was $0 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ , the maximum output voltage and power of the Device-1.2 at $2 4 . 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ reached to $0 . 8 4 4 6 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and $0 . 5 9 4 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ , respectively over $1 . 2 ~ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ optimal load resistance. The electrical output acquisition experiment of Device-2.1 demonstrated maximum $0 . 2 1 0 5 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ voltage and $0 . 0 3 6 9 \mu \mathrm { W }$ power at $3 7 0 . 9 \mathrm { H z }$ resonant frequency over $1 . 2 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ optimal load resistance. The measured results are consistent with the predicted results from the COMSOL simulations. The proposed C-PEHs Device1.1 and 2.1 effectively achieves higher power output compared with similar active area and volume based most popular trapezoidal shaped C-PEHs such as Device-1.2 and 2.2, respectively. Moreover, the obtained power densities demonstrated a good performance when compared to the literature survey of base excitation based C-PEHs. In order to scavenge the low base excitation based vibration energy, a brass proof mass is used at free cantilever ends of the Device-1.1 and 1.2. The testing results also demonstrated that Axe-Head shaped C-PEHs can have the feasibility to recharge wireless mouse battery or supply the power to the low-powerhungry electronics devices.

Cachar- 788010, Assam, India in the year of 2017.
